name: Library of Alexandria, Egypt
issues: 'burned four times across seven centuries' and the 642 AD destruction are not established: Wikipedia records a gradual decline over centuries; the 642 burning-on-Omar's-order story comes from Arabic sources written ~600 years later (al-Qifti, before 1248) and historians have been sceptical of it since Renaudot (1713).
'the ancient world's greatest library' -> 'one of the largest' (source wording).

fix.ctx: One of the largest libraries of the ancient world. It declined gradually over centuries: damage in Caesar's fire (48 BC), the Brucheion quarter destroyed in the 270s and again in 297, the Serapeum daughter library destroyed in 391. The story that it was burned on Caliph Omar's order after the Arab conquest of 642 first appears in Arabic sources ~600 years later and is doubted by historians.

sources.what: Wikipedia (uncontested basics): gradual decline; 297 Brucheion; 642 story from al-Qifti, scepticism since 1713

'Tigris ran black with ink' is a chronicle account ('was said to have'), attributed, not documented.

fix.ctx: Abbasid library and academy in Baghdad, destroyed in the Mongol siege of 1258. Chroniclers record that so many books were thrown into the Tigris that the river was said to run black with ink (chronicle account). No reliable count of its holdings exists.

sources.what: Wikipedia (uncontested basics): 1258 Mongol siege; Tigris ink 'was said to'

fix.ctx: Buddhist monastic university founded in the 5th century CE; likely attacked and ransacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji's forces c. 1200 CE. Its library's size is unknown - estimated in the hundreds of thousands of volumes; the popular 'nine million manuscripts' has no documentary source.

sources.what: Wikipedia (uncontested basics): c. 1200 Khalji; library 'hundreds of thousands', exact number unknown

fix.ctx: An estimated 2.3 million blocks (~6 million tonnes). Built c. 2560 BC. Sides aligned to the cardinal points within a few arcminutes; star-sighting methods that achieve this are documented in the Egyptological literature.

sources.what: Wikipedia (uncontested basics): 2.3 million blocks; alignment methods

'Technology that shouldn't exist at the stated date' unsupported.
Wikipedia: built AD 536-600, andesite/sandstone, Cu-As-Ni bronze cramps; altitude ~3,850 m (12,600 ft) is fine.

fix.ctx: Terraced platform mound of the Tiwanaku culture, built c. AD 536-600, faced with finely cut andesite and sandstone blocks - including the interlocking 'H-blocks' - joined with cast copper-arsenic-nickel cramps. ~3,850 m (12,600 ft) altitude. Claims of machine-precision tolerances and anachronistic technology come from ancient-astronaut literature and have no archaeological support.

'No modern crane can replicate the placement' is false/unsupported - modern heavy-lift cranes exceed these loads; no source offered.
Omits the larger quarry stones (~1,200 t and the 2014 find).

fix.ctx: Trilithon: three limestone blocks of ~800 t each, each over 19 m long, set in the Temple of Jupiter podium. In the nearby quarry lie the Stone of the Pregnant Woman (~1,000 t) and still larger unused blocks (~1,200 t and a block found in 2014). How Roman builders moved them is studied, not unexplained.

sources.what: Wikipedia (uncontested basics): 800 t trilithon; 1,000 t and 1,200 t quarry stones

name: Göbekli Tepe, Turkey
issues: 'Pre-12,000 years old' contradicts its own '9500 BC' (= ~11,450 BP).
'Deliberately buried by its builders' was Klaus Schmidt's preliminary model, since abandoned: Wikipedia - structures repeatedly collapsed, were inundated by landslides and rebuilt.
'The oldest known temple' - no definitive purpose established; 'popularly described as' the first temples; domestic structures found.
'intentionally hidden' unsupported.

fix.ctx: Pre-Pottery Neolithic site occupied c. 9500-8000 BCE (~11,500 years ago), with large circular enclosures of carved T-shaped limestone pillars. Popularly called the 'world's first temple', but no definitive purpose has been established. Schmidt's early idea that it was deliberately backfilled has been revised: the enclosures repeatedly collapsed, were buried by landslides and were rebuilt.

sources.what: Wikipedia (uncontested basics): 9500-8000 BCE; landslides; purpose undetermined; Schmidt model abandoned

Monte Verde II, dated ~14,500 years ago and largely accepted, showed people were in South America at least ~1,000 years before Clovis and overturned the 'Clovis first' model after years of resistance. An older layer (MV-I, ~18,500 cal BP) remains contested.

fix.ctx: One of the world's largest atolls by land area (~312 km2). Cook landed on Christmas Eve 1777. The US detonated 24 devices nearby in 1962 (Operation Dominic). Islanders were usually not evacuated.

fix.ctx: Greenwood District, Tulsa - 'Black Wall Street', one of the wealthiest Black communities in the US. On 31 May-1 June 1921 white mobs, many deputised by city officials, burned more than 35 square blocks. Eyewitnesses describe private aircraft firing on and firebombing the district (attributed). Deaths: official count 36, estimates up to ~300; about 10,000 left homeless; property losses of ~$2.25M (1921). The National Guard interned up to 6,000 Black residents. A grand jury indicted more than 85 people but no one was convicted for the killings or destruction. The survivors' lawsuit was dismissed in 2024; in 2025 the city announced a $105M private trust for descendants.

fix.ctx: Oaklawn Cemetery, Tulsa. Eyewitness accounts describe victims of the 1921 massacre buried in unmarked graves, dumped in the river or burned (attributed). The official death toll was 36 (26 Black, 10 white); estimates run to ~300. In October 2020 a forensic team unearthed 11 coffins in a suspected mass grave; later excavations recovered remains with gunshot wounds. Identification continues more than a century later.

Under martial law detainees needed identification cards and release required a white person to vouch for them; meanwhile homes were looted and burned. Guardsmen fired on Black neighbourhoods, including with a machine gun (attributed).
